However, deploying an auto-regressive guardrail model remains challenging: such models incur high inference latency and are often poorly aligned with customized policies. To address these problems, we present Jev-Guard, a unified model for safety classification and policy routing. We further construct a policy tree over which Jev-Guard performs routing, spanning diverse domains including content moderation, cybersecurity, privacy, and legal compliance. Specifically, Jev-Guard first navigates the policy tree to select the applicable audit policy given the caller's audit context, and then performs safety classification conditioned on the retrieved policies. On 7,033 evaluation cases, Jev-Guard achieves 93.72\% safety accuracy, a mean latency of 58ms, and 93.10\% hierarchical routing accuracy. The full routing-and-classification pipeline averages 240ms. Furthermore, we integrate Jev-Guard into the Hermes harness framework. Across agent trajectories, its separate permission gate cuts mean review time per task from 4.80s for an SFT-LLM judge to 1.33s, with no policy violations are observed for either guard.
screen_reason: own-model: "93.72% safety accuracy, a mean latency of 58ms" on 7,033 cases

title: Delegating Earth science model calibration to knowledge-guided LLM agents
all_authors: Zhanliang Zhu; Ziwei Li; Liujun Zhu; Yuchen Liu; Junliang Jin; Jianyun Zhang
abstract: Applying process-based Earth science models to new sites and questions often requires expert calibration decisions. Reliable delegation to language-model agents must preserve scientific competence and reproducibility. Here we develop a general calibration harness (GCH) for end-to-end delegation from a calibration request to assessed results. Constrained by a knowledge infrastructure (KI) and a validation convention, agents define parameter domains, observation mappings and objectives, and generate model-specific code. GCH checks the formulations against the same declarations and freezes them before numerical search and assessment, which require no further agent judgement. Agent-authored workflows executed across six model families, with assessment identifying unmet criteria. In snow-model tests, five of five knowledge-guided specifications executed on the first attempt, compared with none of five given only the model name, achieving validation Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.81-0.94 against 0.57 for defaults. Under a common objective, independent GR4J formulations yielded scores within 0.001 NSE; re-evaluating eleven saved parameter vectors reproduced their metrics. In ten paired VIC tests with matched budgets, fixed search was non-inferior to continuing agent proposals (margin, -0.02 NSE; median difference, -0.003). This separation enables end-to-end calibration delegation with inspectable scientific choices and reproducible numerical evaluation.
screen_reason: other: Earth science calibration with LLM agents; no typed decision model

title: PRISM: Calibrating Black-Box Judges with Counterfactual Probes
all_authors: Kakei Yamamoto; So Kuroki
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity model motivates representing these responses as a surrogate Jacobian. Ridge regression on human labels learns a correction to the baseline score. The resulting scoring protocol is rubric-free: it uses overall scores without requesting criterion-level ratings. In the main Jev and Sol comparisons on SummEval summarization and HANNA story evaluation, PRISM and its learned-baseline variant significantly improve agreement with human rankings over uncalibrated scores while remaining competitive with rubric-based methods. A controlled SummEval comparison yields similar agreement for rubric-derived quality probes and style probes, supporting calibration without reproducing rubric criteria. The learned coefficients reveal shared and opposing correction directions across judges.
screen_reason: application: PRISM applied to Jev and Sol judges; improves agreement with human rankings on SummEval and HANNA

title: Recalibrating Many Questions with Few Labels: Minimax Rates and Identification Limits
all_authors: Xiaoyu Li; Chiwun Yang
abstract: Many related prediction problems, which we call questions, come with few labels each. What information can be shared across them, and what is actually necessary for good decisions? We answer both for recalibration, motivated by decision models such as Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) that return a probability for any yes/no question a developer writes. A predictor reports a probability $P$ with output law $μ$ on $m$ questions, each with $n$ labels and a nondecreasing map $g_j(p)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid P=p)$; the compound risk is the excess Brier score over the true maps, averaged over questions. Over maps within sup-distance $τ\le 1$ and total variation $V\le 2$ of one nondecreasing shape (fixed effects), the minimax compound risk is $(mn)^{-2/3}+\min\{τ^2,1/n\}+\min\{τ^2,V^2,(V/n)^{2/3}\}$ up to universal constants, for every non-atomic $μ$. A pooled isotonic fit with a per-question correction sized once, on held-out labels of all questions, attains it without knowing $τ$, $V$ or $μ$ ($n\ge 2$, $m\ge 3$); tuning each question on its own labels loses a factor of order $\min\{n,\log(m^2/n)\}$ when the maps differ by constants and $m^2/n$ is large. When the maps are drawn from an unknown prior (random effects), other questions need not identify the Bayes rule. The loss, the identification regret, is at most $2^{-n}$ once the law of a question's data is known, extending a bound of Skibinsky (1968) for coins, and in the worst case at least $β_\star^{-n}/(72\sqrt{n})$ at every finite $m$, where $β_\star\approx 3.583$. Beyond a few labels per question, what cannot be learned is nearly unnecessary. For constant maps (an uninformative predictor) and constant-map priors, the exponential base is exactly $β_\star$, not the 4 suggested by the moment range; for monotone maps it lies in $[2,β_\star]$.
screen_reason: other: Pure minimax theory for recalibration; Jev is only motivation and no measured quantity for a model is reported

title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments
all_authors: Linhai Ma; Yan Wang; Lingfei Qian; Yupeng Cao; Victor Gutierrez Basulto
abstract: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. We call this drop in acceptance the derivation gap. It appears across all seven judges we evaluate, including System One models CLM and Jev. The gap is not only a truncation artifact: correct default values have the largest gap on a benchmark with no truncation. A controlled source-relocation test shows that judges follow the reference in their input: they favor a visible incorrect value over a correct value whose source is hidden. We introduce DeRef (Derived Reference): a separate model reads the full history without seeing the candidate and writes a reference for the judge. Across three benchmarks, DeRef improves overall argument AUROC for all judges tested. On the controlled test, it raises AUROC from chance or below to between 98.40 and 99.59.
screen_reason: evaluation: Derivation gap appears "across all seven judges", including System One models CLM and Jev; AUROC reported

title: How Reliable Are System-One Decisions in Medicine? A Comparative Study of Jev, Jev-like Models, and LLMs
all_authors: Yanrui Du; Danyang Zhao; Sendong Zhao; Wenhao Li; Yibo Gao; Haochun Wang; Zhuoer Xu; Shiwen Cui; Bing Qin
abstract: Jev has attracted considerable attention for its rapid, generalizable decision-making, yet its medical reliability remains underexplored. To address this gap, our study compares various types of system-one decision models across 15 medical datasets comprising 8,742 instances under a unified protocol. Beyond accuracy, we assess decision stability and the ability to recognize unreliable decisions. Our results show that Jev rivals leading models on primarily text-driven tasks but is less effective on numerically driven tasks, revealing a distinct capability boundary. Under question-format variations, Jev maintains strong decision consistency and small accuracy fluctuations. StartLux-27B exhibits comparable consistency, while D3-27B achieves higher overall accuracy and a lower mean decision reversal rate. But these strengths do not extend to reliable abstention awareness: most evaluated models show limitations in both recognizing missing correct answers and using optional abstention. Moreover, we find that Jev's probability-based answer selection can be improved by changing how decisions are scored: normalizing option-wise binary scores yields higher retained accuracy than choice scoring. Taken together, our findings provide early guidance for improving and applying decision models in medicine.
screen_reason: evaluation: Compares system-one models across 15 medical datasets on accuracy, stability and abstention

title: Reading Right, Acting Wrong: Diagnosing Decision Failures of System One Models in Agent Loops
all_authors: Yubo Li; Ramayya Krishnan; Rema Padman
abstract: System One models choose an agent's next action by scoring a supplied set of options in a single pass. This makes them fast and cheap, but when they choose wrongly there is nothing to inspect: did the model misread what the agent has seen, or read it correctly and still act wrongly? We answer behaviorally. On a frozen benchmark of agent decision states from simulated environments, customer-service policies, tool use, web navigation and coding, we pair every next-action question with factual probes about the same state, each answered independently. Across seventeen fast systems and a reasoning model, the answer is consistent: most wrong actions follow correct reading, and the more accurate a system, the more of its errors take this form. These errors are not noise; they gather on the same states across systems of every kind. Where the probed facts provably determine the action, models that read every fact still fail to combine them, and their own answers, composed by code, repair the failure. On real states, what is missing is often not a fact but the next sub-goal.
screen_reason: evaluation: Diagnoses decision failures across seventeen fast systems on a frozen agent-state benchmark

title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models
all_authors: Kawai Chung; Chunkit Chan; Yuxuan Liu; Yauwai Yim; Xi Yang; Wenbin Hu; Huihao Jing; Chiu Yeung Tang; Changxuan Fan; Ki Sen Hung; Tsun On Kwok; Haoran Li
abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.
screen_reason: evaluation: Jev "reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy" on 11,117 ToM questions

title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
all_authors: Yang Luo; Tiantian Ji; Zifeng Kang; Yucheng Wang; Yong Liu; Zhiyi Yin; Xinran Liu
abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).
screen_reason: evaluation: JevProbe: 81.5% of 228 real-world Jev applications show decision flips

title: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction
all_authors: Yuhan Zhu; Xiangyu Zeng; Qingyi Si; Chenxu Yang; Yifei Li; Luozheng Qin; Junhao Zhou; Dingyu Yao; Jun Zhang; Chuanyu Qin; Zhiqiu Zhang; Yuandong Yang; Yuqi Xu; Tianyu Zhang; Hongcheng Guo; Jiaqi Wang; Nan Duan; Limin Wang
abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
screen_reason: own-model: Video System One family; mIoU gains of 6.7 and 10.8 points and inference speedups of 2.8-3.1x

title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
all_authors: Qi Li; Xinchao Wang
abstract: System one models like Jev enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent open-source practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations against Jev and open source models, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.
screen_reason: own-model: Decision-native architecture compared against Jev and open models; "no decision flips under any tested permutations"

title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
all_authors: Xiaoguang Guo; Yaohao Long; Chuxu Zhang
abstract: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair. These findings inform a global diagnosis that considers all execution steps. Without reference answers, BLADE achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies under a shared Jev decision interface on 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 percentage points. Making responsibility evidence explicit offers a path toward more interpretable and reliable agentic systems.
screen_reason: application: BLADE uses Jev for probabilistic judgments; best step accuracy among eight strategies on 1,228 failed runs

title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
all_authors: Yifan Lan; Zhongye Liu; Yurui Chang; Hanyu Wang; Yongkang Du; Lu Lin; Jinghui Chen
abstract: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.
screen_reason: evaluation: DecisionRobust benchmark evaluates 30 text and 17 vision configurations under attack

title: When Is Smaller Greener? Right-Sizing Language Models for Agentic AI
all_authors: Sajid Siraj; Maria Barbati
abstract: AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to plan and act over multiple steps, yet models are usually compared per call rather than per completed task. This paper asks: which model should an agent use to complete tasks reliably while minimising energy, cost and time? We show that per-call comparisons can be misleading for agentic AI. Because a task succeeds only if all required steps succeed, small differences in per-step reliability can produce large differences in overall task success. Failed attempts also consume resources. We therefore evaluate models using energy, cost and time per successfully completed task, treating the completed task as the functional unit. On this basis, we develop a decision model for choosing LLMs in agentic workflows. The model applies to tasks with binary or graded outcomes and to settings with or without retries. We show that each resource has a crossover task length at which a smaller, less reliable model ceases to be the greener, cheaper or faster option. These crossovers divide tasks into three regimes: for short tasks smaller models are preferred, for long tasks larger models are preferred, and only between these extremes do preferences among objectives matter. We embed these results in a two-stage framework that separates efficiency from preference. A Pareto screen first removes models that are never competitive; a weighted decision is required only when a genuine trade-off remains. A pilot study of 15 open-weight models from five developers, ranging from 0.6B to 27B parameters, on two multi-step agent tasks with measured GPU energy supports the predicted structure. The model with the lowest energy per completed task changes with task length and task type, and observed crossover points generally match those predicted from per-step measurements. These findings provide a practical framework for right-sizing language models in agentic AI.
screen_reason: other: Uses "decision model" for choosing LLMs in agentic workflows (energy/cost analysis); unrelated sense

title: AgriJev: Efficient Agricultural Candidate Scoring with Multi-Scale Adapted Models
all_authors: Xuechen Li
abstract: Agricultural systems make decisions over heterogeneous entity types, textual judgments, and knowledge-question options. Generating a textual answer adds decoding and extraction steps to decisions that ultimately require a candidate choice. We introduce AgriJev, a family of adapted Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B. A shared interface conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, returning scores and relative probabilities in one forward call. We prepare source-aware training records and frozen evaluations from existing agricultural resources, retaining original groups and annotation provenance. Comparisons include original Qwen3.5 models and matched agricultural SFT models, both evaluated through native answer generation. Across 17 external test views, AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy, exceeding the original and SFT generators by 5.89 and 3.79 percentage points. It outperforms the original generator on 13 views and narrows the mean gap to hosted Jev 1.13.0. On a fixed A100 workload, its median scoring latency is approximately half that of same-scale answer generation. Task-dependent gains and failures characterize a practical choice among agricultural model weights and inference contracts.
screen_reason: own-model: Returns scores and probabilities "in one forward call"; AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy

title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
all_authors: Baowen Zhang; Hangting Ye; Hongyuan Zha
abstract: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.
screen_reason: evaluation: "compare four decision models with three large language models"; reports accuracy, cost, robustness to 21 rewrites

title: JevCoder: When Does Decision Delegation Pay Off in Code Repair?
all_authors: Jiahao Zhang; Yifan Zhang; Yu Huang
abstract: A coding agent repeatedly makes decisions as it repairs code. These decisions shape repair trajectories and affect the token cost of successive model requests. We ask which repair decisions can be delegated to a low-cost probabilistic judge to reduce token use while maintaining repair quality. The judges answer questions with probabilities over predefined answers, without generating explanations. We evaluate judgment quality across repair stages and test how individual interventions change subsequent repair work. We compare these interventions with unguided repair, which uses no judge, and with the same workflow using the repair model itself as the judge. The benefit depends on the work an intervention changes, rather than the cost of the judgment alone. Based on these studies, we propose JevCoder, a workflow built around Jev, a low-cost probabilistic judge. It combines code-snippet recommendations with action-type guidance and uses judgments to determine when to submit. We evaluate three repair models, each on the same 400 tasks: 200 from SWE-bench Verified and 200 from SWE-Bench Pro Verified. Compared to unguided repair, JevCoder reduces mean repair-model token use by 21.6%-50.6%, with higher observed repair rates across all three models.
screen_reason: application: "JevCoder... built around Jev"; reports judgment quality and 21.6%-50.6% token reduction on 400 tasks

title: Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev
all_authors: Ilaria Imperatrice; Taisia Kameneva; Adam Eric Greenberg; Alessandro Romano
abstract: Do AI models designed for fast, structured decisions exhibit the cognitive and social biases observed in human judgment? We evaluate Jev, a model described as a System One decision-maker, using 41,500 responses across cognitive reflection tasks, five classical cognitive-bias paradigms, and a pricing experiment testing ethnic and gender bias. At the level of selected answers, the results are largely encouraging. We confirm previous findings that Jev performs extremely well on cognitive reflection problems. We also observe that it generally avoids the characteristic choice patterns associated with several well-documented human biases, and exhibits only small differences among demographic groups in the tested pricing scenario. However, this apparent robustness conceals important vulnerabilities. Its judgments are sensitive to irrelevant numerical information and the ordering of response options. Moreover, several cognitive-bias manipulations substantially affect returned probabilities even when selected answers remain unchanged. Most strikingly, Jev answers a well-known probability problem correctly in every response but violates the same underlying probability rule in every response to an adapted version. We investigate this discrepancy using 15,000 additional responses across 30 conjunction tasks. Jev violates the rule in 54\% of responses, with accuracy varying dramatically across formulations and answer orders. These findings suggest that evaluating decision models solely on familiar benchmarks and selected answers may substantially overstate their reliability in practical applications. They also identify vulnerabilities for developers to address and practical considerations for users integrating such models into automated decision-making systems.
screen_reason: evaluation: "We evaluate Jev... using 41,500 responses"; bias, order sensitivity, probability shifts

title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
all_authors: Bin Zheng; Zheng Chen
abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.
screen_reason: own-model: trains reader returning distributions over candidates; "accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%"

title: Calibration and Risk-Budgeted Decisions with System One Models
all_authors: Soundouss Messoudi; Youness Mansar
abstract: LLM workflows and agents rely on a set of binary decisions like allow/block an input, or discard/retain a retrieved document. When human deferral is unavailable, uncertain cases must still receive an action. We study System One decision scores in this setting by defaulting to a conservative fallback when uncertain, and controlling the false omission risk within the subset of inputs assigned the utility-maximizing action. Across six datasets covering moderation, safety, and reranking, we compare general System One models with task baselines and a local open-weights fine-tuned System One model. We show that naive baselines for threshold selection exceed the target risk in roughly half of settings with defined test risk, compared with 7.8\% for Learn Then Test (LTT), which leverages finite-sample statistical guarantees. Our results show why relying on a probability-like interface is insufficient for deployment decisions and how risk-budgeted selection trades useful action against observed error.
screen_reason: evaluation: "we compare general System One models with task baselines"; calibration and risk-control results across six datasets

title: Lost in the Fallback: How Reliably Do Typed Decision Models Use Fallback Options?
all_authors: Yuanbo Xie; Mingli Zhu; Tianyun Liu; Yingjie Zhang; Haixiao Xiong; Tingwen Liu
abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) are increasingly used in applications such as request routing and model selection, making reliable decisions critical to system performance. Fallback options accommodate categories outside regular choices, enabling deferral to human experts or more capable models. While recent works have examined adversarial vulnerabilities in TDMs, their ability to follow fallback rules in non-adversarial settings remains underexplored. We introduce the Paired Fallback Robustness (PFR) Test to evaluate two aspects of fallback reliability: whether models correctly switch between regular and fallback options, and whether they make consistent decisions under logically equivalent definitions of the same rule. We evaluate open-source decision models on three benchmarks, with controlled comparisons across architectures and parameter counts. We find that correct recognition does not reliably transfer to correct fallback options, and errors persist even when the correct category is explicitly supplied.Moreover, logically equivalent formulations of the same fallback rule can also produce substantial disagreement in model decisions. These findings reveal a crucial reliability gap in current TDMs: fallback mechanisms designed to improve reliability can instead introduce errors. It highlights faithful execution of fallback rules and consistency under equivalent definitions as essential requirements for reliable typed decision-making.
screen_reason: evaluation: "We evaluate open-source decision models on three benchmarks" with the PFR test

title: Occupancy Modeling via Drifting: One-Step Generation Enables Direct Policy Extraction
all_authors: Robin Uhrich; Marco Bagatella; Núria Armengol Urpí; Pavel Kolev; Georg Martius
abstract: The growing interest in behavior foundation models, combined with recent advancements in generative modeling, has led to an appealing recipe for reinforcement learning from unlabeled data: pre-train a generative model to model occupancies, i.e., discounted state visitations, on reward-free trajectories, such that a policy can be easily extracted once a small reward-labeled dataset becomes available. We decompose this recipe along three axes: (i) the degree to which the multi-modal structure of occupancies must be captured, (ii) the class of generative model, and (iii) the method used for policy extraction. Along each axis, we consider existing choices, propose simpler alternatives, and validate each decision experimentally. This analysis culminates in a novel, streamlined method that leverages drifting, a modern one-step generative sampler, to model the occupancy. We show that this enables policy extraction via direct differentiation through the occupancy model, and bypasses the need for critic distillation. Overall, we observe that this nimble setup leads to improvements in performance on standard benchmarks.
screen_reason: other: "nimble" used as an adjective; offline RL occupancy modeling, unrelated

title: Diagnose Before You Refine: Multi-Dimensional Judge Feedback for Query-Efficient Jailbreak Attacks
all_authors: Yixin Tan; Chia-Yi Hsu; Jiayang Liu; Chia-Mu Yu; Rui Wen
abstract: Automated jailbreak attacks rely on evaluation feedback to optimize adversarial prompts, but existing methods often lack fine-grained diagnostic information. We propose Jev-Guided Strategy Bandit (JSB), a query-based jailbreak framework that leverages multi-dimensional probabilistic feedback to guide prompt optimization. JSB combines continuous jailbreak scoring with targeted refinement, strategy switching, and best-state reseeding to balance exploration and refinement. We evaluate JSB on two harmful request datasets across five open-source and three closed-source LLMs. Under a budget of only 10 target-model queries, JSB achieves an average HarmBench attack success rate of 89.8\% across ten open-source settings, consistently outperforming existing automated jailbreak attacks. Further analyses demonstrate its effectiveness under varying query budgets and attacker models. Defense experiments also reveal limitations in existing filtering mechanisms and highlight the potential of Jev-based output filtering.
screen_reason: application: "Jev-Guided Strategy Bandit"; Jev as probabilistic judge, ASR 89.8% and "Jev-based output filtering" defense experiments (borderline: measured quantity is attack success)

title: Jev-as-a-Judge for RAG Claim Verification: Confidence-Gated Cascading Between a Non-Generative Verifier and a Frontier LLM
all_authors: Alden Do Rosario; Kirollos Atef
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation asks one question at volume: does this evidence support this claim? The answer is one bit, yet most pipelines obtain it from a text generator and pay generation prices for the prose wrapped around it. We compare a non-generative decision model, which returns a typed value from a declared enumeration together with a native probability and no text, against a frontier LLM configured as an engineer would deploy it for binary classification. Both answer the same 495 human-labelled claims from LLM-AggreFact, so every comparison is within-item. We report three things. First, the two systems are statistically indistinguishable on the metric this task is conventionally scored by, a paired difference of -0.56 points, Jev minus Astra, at a 187-fold cost difference. Second, that tie carries almost no information about deployment: the systems disagree on 15.2% of claims, and the cheaper one admits 23.2% of the claims annotators marked unsupported against the frontier model's 14.1%. A component whose job is to catch unsupported claims should be judged on that rate, and the conventional headline hides it. Third, because the errors differ they compose: routing the claims the cheap model is confident about and escalating the rest reaches 74.10 at USD 2.92 per thousand claims against 73.83 at USD 8.93, with the threshold chosen out of fold. But a matched random-escalation control at in-sample thresholds, spending the same budget by coin flip, does as well, so what buys the saving is the escalation share and not the probability that picks what to escalate. Measured against the cheap model it is built from, the cascade costs 61-fold more for 0.83 points, 95% CI [-3.36, 4.86], and it is the more permissive guard of the two. Equal accuracy conceals unequal errors. All predictions, prompts, pricing and code are released.
screen_reason: evaluation: Non-generative decision model vs frontier LLM on 495 claims: paired accuracy, 187-fold cost, confidence-gated cascade result

title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
all_authors: Ningxin Pan; Hanyu Li; Yeqing Shen; Ning Ding; Yehui Tang; Wentao Zhang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.
screen_reason: application: "the faster Jev"; "raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19" (borderline: Jev used as fast game agent, abstract does not state probability output)

title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
all_authors: Avdhesh Singh Chouhan; Jack Perry
abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.
screen_reason: own-model: "Verdict-MQ, an open encoder"; KL 0.080 vs 0.117 for Laya, Jev zero-shot reference measured

title: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
all_authors: Qianlong Lan; Anuj Kaul; Vinothini Pandurangan; Indranil Sanyal
abstract: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. Recent probabilistic decision models aim to support such decisions through calibrated confidence estimates, but their reliability under distribution shift remains uncertain. We evaluate a native probabilistic decision model (Jev), two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers (22M and 86M), and an LLM-based judge on 47,611 held-out examples spanning direct and indirect prompt injections, hard-benign inputs, obfuscation, and distribution shift. Using separate development and calibration splits, we assess detection performance, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol. The LLM judge achieves the highest overall discrimination (AUROC 0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714). However, Jev's native probabilities do not consistently outperform post-hoc calibrated classifier scores, and temperature scaling improves calibration without improving discrimination. At an empirical false-negative-rate target of 1%, all evaluated gate-reviewer systems require more than 91.8% escalation and incur substantial false-positive rates. These findings demonstrate that probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift. Effective LLM security systems must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.

title: Prune the Summary, Not the History: Source-Judged Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
all_authors: Guanghui Min; Chen Chen
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction: when the interaction history outgrows the context window, a compressor replaces it with a natural-language summary. We show that these summaries contain more than a record of what happened. Compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, so each summary mixes facts established by the environment with reasoning written by the compressor, and the agent cannot tell the two apart afterwards. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, 83% of failed runs trace back to an action that carries out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports. We propose Source-Judged Compaction (SJC), a training-free post-processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it has a source in the environment outputs or the previous summary, and removes the entries that do not. It changes neither the agent nor the compressor and adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction. The judge is Jev, a non-generative decision model that answers the source question with a calibrated probability instead of text. On AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1%-8.9% without increasing the agent's token usage.
screen_reason: application: "The judge is Jev, a non-generative decision model"; SJC improves reliability 2.1%-8.9%

title: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models
all_authors: Dingjie Song; Zhiling Yan; Yuxuan Zhang; Lichao Sun
abstract: Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual-process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On-demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.
screen_reason: own-model: "We present LEV, a decision model"; 63.2% to 76.2% on JevBench, latency below 50 ms

title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
all_authors: Dingjie Song; Zhiling Yan; Ziqian Zhang; Yuxuan Zhang; Lichao Sun
abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.
screen_reason: application: "cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds"; PremiseCheck accuracy near GPT-5.5 at half cost

title: When to Ask for Help: A Decision-Theoretic Account and Measurement Standard for Slow-Module Scheduling in Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Models
all_authors: Shilin Zhang
abstract: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $ρ$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $ρ$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$ρ$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($ρ=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
